prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles Eyelids, fall softly, from their gritted corners chalk, let it drizzle, let the streams flow thick with a waste glaze, let imagery run off its surplus of kaolin, choke feed of sediment plumed into the blue, tulipping its stem. Cress bunches thickening in shallows, flukes stinging flank heifers in their shove and jostle down a bank, drinking, mud caking lips. Eyelids, fall softly, let me linger interrupted behind the curtains billowing with images, how the unseeable sill even so snags, how the very point lights from behind, thoughts dispersing into folds slung aloft in sea mist, impermissible point breaks every motive falling back behind the eyelids that then fall. I breathe, I look, I carry forward, I can sense the last of you, taking walks of air thick with waste breath your form displaces. O curtain! O rail! I hate the thick floor beneath, breathe over a market quarrel, rise over the bass sawing at its stems to crash down the vault, let the vault branch recklessly, light-streams maze, air’s stirring carry song back and forth; I hear your recorder pipe, long for its repeats giving what-for to earth seeming to attenuate, rock is marked with your aeolian flow. Eyelids, fall softly, the cast of their fluttering fans across the inlet a white shadow, writes over deep-set floor captivated ripples. World, gaze out! Rise from a shrouded point.

outputs.L1:
In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles

Eyelids, fall softly; from their gritted corners, chalk—let it drizzle, let the streams run thick with a waste glaze, let imagery shed its surplus of kaolin, a choke-feed of sediment pluming into the blue, tulipping its stem. Cress bunches thicken in the shallows; flukes sting the flanks of heifers as they shove and jostle down the bank, drinking, mud caking their lips.

Eyelids, fall softly; let me linger, interrupted, behind curtains billowing with images: how the unseeable sill nevertheless snags; how the very point is lit from behind; thoughts dispersing into folds slung aloft in sea mist; an impermissible point breaking every motive, falling back behind the eyelids that then fall.

I breathe, I look, I carry forward; I can sense the last of you, taking walks through air thick with the waste breath your form displaces. O curtain! O rail! I hate the thick floor beneath; breathe over a market quarrel; rise over the bass sawing at its stems to crash down the vault; let the vault branch recklessly, light-streams mazing, air’s stirring carrying song back and forth. I hear your recorder pipe, long for its repetitions giving what-for to earth, seeming to attenuate; rock is marked with your aeolian flow.

Eyelids, fall softly; the cast of their fluttering fans across the inlet—a white shadow—writes over deep-set floor, captivated ripples.

World, gaze out! Rise from a shrouded point.
outputs.L2:
For Sara Wilkinson, remembered, and for Liz Miles

Let the eyelids descend gently. From their clenched edges, a chalky powder loosens—let it fall like rain, let the currents grow heavy with a glazed residue. Let the images shed their excess kaolin, a strangled surge of silt feathering into the blue, opening like a tulip on its stalk.

In the shallows, clusters of cress grow dense. Gadflies sting the sides of young cows as they crowd and push one another down the bank to drink, their mouths crusted with mud.

Eyelids, lower softly. Let me remain for a while, delayed behind curtains swollen with pictures: how even the unseen ledge catches, how the sharpest point is lit from behind, how thoughts scatter into raised folds of sea fog. That forbidden point interrupts every intention, sending it back behind the eyelids as they close.

I inhale, I watch, I go on carrying what remains. I can still feel the last trace of you, moving through air made dense by spent breath, your body shifting it aside.

O curtain, O railing—how I loathe the heavy floor below. Breathe above the argument in the marketplace. Rise above the bass as it saws through its own stems and brings the vault crashing down. Let that vault split into wild branches; let streams of light turn labyrinthine; let the moving air bear song back and forth. I hear the pipe of your recorder and yearn for its repetitions, its rebuke to an earth that seems to thin away. Stone itself is inscribed by your wind-borne current.

Eyelids, fall gently. The sweep of their trembling fans casts a pale shadow across the inlet, writing over the deep floor’s entranced ripples.

World, look outward. Lift yourself from the veiled point.
outputs.L3:
The poem mourns and memorializes Sara Wilkinson while also addressing Liz Miles, creating a layered act of remembrance that is both private and shared. Its elegiac tone suggests that the speaker is trying to honor someone who has died while also reaching out to someone still present, perhaps as a witness or fellow mourner. This dual address gives the poem an intimate emotional structure: it is not only about loss, but also about the relationships that remain around that loss.

A repeated request for the eyelids to “fall softly” becomes one of the poem’s central gestures. This phrase suggests the closing of the eyes, but it does not simply imply sleep or withdrawal. Instead, it marks a movement inward, toward memory, grief, and imagination. By asking the eyelids to fall gently, the speaker seems to seek a tender way of seeing what can no longer be seen directly. The closed eye becomes a space where the absent person may still be encountered through recollection, dream, or inward vision.

The poem’s natural imagery reinforces this emotional movement. Images of water, sediment, mist, animals, and light create a world that is unstable, fluid, and constantly shifting. Water and sediment suggest depth, disturbance, and what settles after motion; mist obscures clear outlines; animals introduce instinctive life and movement; light offers moments of perception or revelation. Together, these images convey emotional turbulence and the difficulty of finding stillness in grief. The natural world does not simply provide a background for mourning; it mirrors the speaker’s inner state.

At the same time, the poem suggests that the absent person has not entirely disappeared. The speaker senses a lingering presence through breath, sound, air, and remembered movement. These subtle traces make absence feel strangely active. Sara Wilkinson is gone, yet something of her seems to remain in the atmosphere of the poem, carried by sensory impressions that cannot be fully grasped. Breath and sound are especially important because they are intimate but fleeting: they point to life, voice, and bodily presence, while also emphasizing how fragile those traces have become.

Vision in the poem is presented as both obscured and illuminated. Curtains, shadows, and eyelids shape what can be perceived, suggesting that grief changes the act of seeing. Loss may darken or interrupt vision, but it can also create a different kind of insight. The speaker does not see clearly in an ordinary sense; instead, perception is filtered through memory, imagination, and mourning. The falling eyelids, the shifting light, and the veils of mist and shadow all suggest that loss is understood indirectly, through partial glimpses and inward illumination.

Overall, the poem becomes an elegy that explores how grief transforms perception. It memorializes Sara Wilkinson not by fixing her in a static image, but by evoking her through movement, atmosphere, and sensation. The address to Liz Miles adds a human connection to this act of mourning, while the repeated inward turn of the eyelids suggests that memory may offer a fragile but meaningful way to remain close to the dead.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents grief as a fluid and image-rich experience, one in which the speaker mourns absent loved ones not through direct statement alone but through a sequence of shifting sensory impressions. Images of eyelids, curtains, water, sediment, breath, music, and light create a world where perception is never entirely clear or stable. Seeing becomes blurred by memory, just as memory is shaped by what the body continues to sense. The eyelids and curtains suggest partial vision, concealment, and the fragile boundary between inner and outer worlds. Water and sediment imply depth, movement, and the gradual settling of experience, as though grief leaves behind layers that cannot be easily removed. Breath and music evoke the lingering presence of those who are gone, suggesting that absence may still be felt in rhythm, vibration, and silence. Light, meanwhile, both reveals and obscures, making the lost figures momentarily visible before they recede again.

Through these interwoven images, the poem suggests that mourning is not a simple process of remembering what has disappeared. Instead, grief becomes a mode of perception. The speaker does not fully recover the dead, but neither are they wholly lost. They remain present in fragments, sensations, and traces: in the movement of air, in the dimness behind closed eyes, in the play of light across surfaces, and in the sounds that seem to echo beyond their source. The poem’s flowing structure reinforces this idea, allowing one image to dissolve into another as if thought, memory, and feeling were all part of the same current.

The key result is a vision of grief as both obscuring and sustaining. Loss clouds the world, making it difficult to see clearly, yet it also keeps the beloved dead perceptible in transformed ways. The poem does not deny absence, but it refuses to treat absence as emptiness. Instead, it shows how memory inhabits the senses and how the dead continue to exist through the impressions they have left behind. In this way, mourning becomes an act of continued attention, turning pain into a form of presence and transforming loss into an ongoing relationship with what can no longer be physically held.
outputs.L5:
Sara Wilkinson had always been the kind of person who noticed small details: the way sunlight fell across the kitchen table, the hesitation in someone’s voice, or the quiet kindness hidden in an ordinary day. Her friend Liz admired that about her. While Liz often rushed from one task to the next, Sara had a way of slowing things down and helping people see what really mattered.

One afternoon, Liz visited Sara Wilkinson at her little house near the edge of town. The two sat together with cups of tea, talking about old memories, future plans, and the unexpected turns life can take. Liz shared her worries about a new job opportunity, unsure whether she was ready for such a big change. Sara listened carefully, then smiled and said, “Sometimes the right path feels uncertain simply because it matters.”

Those words stayed with Liz. With Sara Wilkinson’s encouragement, she found the courage to take the next step. And in that quiet moment between two friends, Liz realized that support does not always come in grand gestures. Sometimes it is found in a conversation, a warm cup of tea, and the steady belief of someone who knows you well.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental elegiac prose poem beginning with the dedication “In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles,” using the recurring phrase “Eyelids, fall softly,” and imagery of clay, water, curtains, breath, music, and light.
counterfactuals.output:
In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles,

Eyelids, fall softly, as curtains fall when the room has finished being a room and becomes instead a blue vessel, a held breath, a bowl of rainwater set on the sill to learn the moon.

We were made of clay first, or so the story says—thumb-marked, hollowed, lifted from the riverbank. And even now the body remembers: the damp weight of grief, the kiln of the chest, the hairline crack where light gets in and refuses to leave. I place my hand there and hear music, not loud, not whole, but the thin note a cup makes when it is touched at the rim.

Eyelids, fall softly. Not like doors. Not like stones. Like linen released from a washing line. Like dusk untying its gold from the windows. Like a mother drawing curtains against the cold, though some cold remains, though some names go on shining under the fabric.

Sara, the water has not stopped speaking. It says your name in gutters, in kettles, in the small flooded fields of the morning. It says what cannot be kept can still be carried. It says every river is an archive of rain. I bend to listen, and my breath clouds the glass between this world and whatever room you have entered.

Liz, I do not know how to offer comfort except to say: the light has changed, but it has not gone. It leans now differently through the curtains. It touches the clay jug, the empty chair, the cup cooling beside the bed. It makes a harp of dust. It makes an altar of the ordinary. It keeps arriving, even when we cannot bear arrival.

Eyelids, fall softly, over the unbearable brightness. Let the body rest from seeing. Let the heart, that dark animal, curl beside the embers. Let music come without hands: a low chord under the floorboards, a remembered voice in the throat of the house, a lullaby the water hums to the clay before it hardens.

And if grief is a room, let it have windows.

And if memory is a window, let it have curtains.

And if love is the hand drawing them open again, let there be morning—  
not sudden, not cruel,  
but pale and patient,  
washing the walls with breath,  
lifting from the earth its tender vessels,  
saying softly, softly:

Eyelids, fall softly.

Then rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, lyrical modernist poem about grief and perception, addressed to the world and to the dead, with surreal pastoral imagery, long flowing sentences, and a refrain involving eyelids falling softly.
counterfactuals.output:
World, you green bewilderment, you field with a fever under its tongue,  
you orchard of clocks ripening in the rain, you road that keeps walking away from the feet that love it,  
I have come to you carrying the dead like a bowl of dark water, and the water keeps remembering their faces,  
and the faces keep breaking under the smallest light.

O dead, you patient listeners behind the milkweed,  
you who have become the inside of bells, the blue pressure in stones, the sleep in the mouths of horses,  
do not think I have ceased to look for you—  
I look in the lamb’s black eye, in the cloud snagged on the steeple,  
in the wheat bending as if a hand has passed over it from another weather,  
and everywhere perception opens its many windows and everywhere grief enters like a bird that has forgotten the sky.

And eyelids fall softly, softly,  
like petals over the wells of seeing.

World, I accuse you of beauty,  
of letting the pear tree stand there in its white delirium while the grave is still fresh,  
of letting the river polish its knives on the stones,  
of letting morning arrive with bread under its arm and no explanation,  
while in me the absent continue their slow work, rearranging the furniture of breath,  
placing a chair beside the window for the one who will not sit.

O dead, do you see how the cows move through the mist like thoughts before language,  
how the hills kneel down in their green dresses, how the scarecrow lifts its straw arms to embrace a thunderhead,  
how the moon, a blind shepherdess, leads her flock of bones across the pasture of night?  
I am learning that to see is to be wounded by distance,  
that each leaf is a small green eyelid trembling over an immeasurable eye,  
that the world is not what it is but what has vanished through it.

And eyelids fall softly, softly,  
like snow over the mouths of wells.

I speak to you, world, through the torn gauze of attention,  
through the bee’s gold engine, through the sheep-bell’s rusted vowel, through the drenched lilac bending under its own memory,  
and I say: take back your distances, your mirrors, your cruel abundance,  
take back the red fox stitched to the dusk, the pond holding the sky like a secret bruise,  
take back the grass that rises after every footfall, innocent, innumerable, unforgiving—  
unless you can return to me one hand, one laugh, one sleeping forehead warm as bread beneath the morning sheet.

But the dead answer only by becoming wider.  
They widen into wind, into pasture, into the silence between two crows.  
They widen until even the smallest room is full of them,  
until the cup on the table glows with their not-being,  
until my own eyes, those two dark animals drinking from the visible,  
grow heavy with all they cannot hold.

And eyelids fall softly, softly,  
like dusk on the backs of grazing sheep.

O dead, beloved unreturning,  
if grief is a country, then I have married its weather;  
if perception is a lantern, then sorrow is the moth that burns and blesses it;  
if the world is a page, then your absence is the ink in which all things are written—  
the barn leaning into its shadow, the plum split open like a small purple heart,  
the rain combing the meadow’s tangled hair,  
the white road dissolving into distance as though distance were mercy.

World, listen: I am still here,  
though here is a word with a hollow center,  
though the day passes through me wearing the faces of those I have lost,  
though the black trees at evening lift their roots into the air and walk toward the sea,  
though the stars arrive like seeds spilled from a dead man’s pocket,  
though every looking is a losing and every loss is lit from within.

And eyelids fall softly, softly,  
like flowers closing over the astonished light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem in the style of contemporary avant-garde ecopoetry: mournful, image-heavy, syntactically intricate, with references to kaolin, cattle at a riverbank, sea mist, a recorder pipe, and a final imperative for the world to gaze out.
counterfactuals.output:
**White Pit Elegy**

In the quarry’s unclosed mouth, kaolin glows—  
not snow, not bone, but the thought of bone  
after rain has rinsed its grammar from the hill,  
after the trucks have learned to speak in reverse  
and the pines, listening, thin themselves into needles  
of accusation.

There were cattle at the riverbank,  
their dark heads lowered as if drinking  
from a wound they had inherited,  
mud flowering around their hooves,  
flies stitching and unstitching the afternoon  
to the flank, the ear, the salt-lit eye—  
and beyond them the river, carrying  
its brown weather seaward,  
each ripple a small refusal of permanence.

Sea mist came inland all night,  
entering the fields like an animal without edges,  
wetting the broken fence, the tin roof,  
the abandoned hive with its waxen lungs,  
and in the orchard the pears softened  
into little planets of surrender.

Who played, then, the recorder pipe  
from the culvert’s green throat—  
that reedy, childlike interval  
threading the drainage ditch,  
as though breath itself, having escaped us,  
had chosen a narrower body  
through which to remember wind?

O clay of the earth’s pale under-tongue,  
O milk-white dust on the hands of extraction,  
O river slick with reflected livestock and sky—  
we have named too much and touched too harshly;  
we have made of the meadow a ledger,  
of the rain a contract,  
of the bird a vanishing unit of song.

Still the mist lifts. Still the cattle turn.  
Still the pipe, somewhere underground,  
keens its thin green weather.

World, gaze out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a memorial poem for Sara Wilkinson and Liz Miles that feels abstract and visionary rather than straightforward—something full of eyelids, curtains, water, sediment, air, song, and the sensation of someone recently gone.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Sara Wilkinson and Liz Miles**

The eyelids of the morning tremble,  
not yet open, not yet closed—  
two curtains breathing in a room  
where no one has touched the chairs.

Water keeps speaking  
under the floorboards of the world.  
It carries the silt of your laughter,  
the fine sediment of hands,  
the shimmer left behind  
when a body steps out of its shape.

Sara—  
Liz—  
your names move like air through gauze,  
not gone, but thinned into weather,  
into the pale song the curtains make  
when the window is barely open.

We listen there.

In the hush after footsteps,  
in the cup’s small echo,  
in the river folding light into itself,  
something of you continues—  
not as a portrait,  
not as a story with its edges tied,  
but as drifting pollen,  
as moonlit water,  
as the invisible wingbeat  
that changes the room.

The earth gathers what it must gather.  
Sediment settles.  
Rain writes over the stones.  
Yet beneath every surface  
a current refuses stillness.

And when our own eyelids lower,  
we see it:  
two figures beyond the last curtain,  
not departing,  
but becoming distance,  
becoming brightness,  
becoming the song  
air remembers  
after the singer is gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph prose poem with no title, opening “In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles,” blending elegy, landscape, and dreamlike visual perception; make it ornate, strange, and emotionally intense.
counterfactuals.output: In memory of Sara Wilkinson and for Liz Miles, the hills at evening loosened their dark hair and let the rain comb through it, each blade of grass carrying a small, unrepeatable light as if the dead had leaned close to breathe on the earth; I walked there in the blue aftermath, where the river kept folding its silver animal back into itself and the trees, stunned into prayer, lifted their blackened hands against a sky of bruised pearl, and everywhere I looked the world was doubled—stone with its ghost-stone, cloud with its drowned twin, my own shadow moving a little ahead of me like someone who had already received the news. In that country grief had the color of foxgloves and old milk, and the air trembled with impossible errands: a door opening in a sheep’s eye, a lantern swinging beneath the skin of the pond, your name written and unwritten by midges above the nettles, until vision itself became a veil embroidered with salt, and through it I saw Sara not as lost but as dispersed—into ash bark, into the wet mouths of mosses, into the cold cup of a primrose holding its yellow flame against oblivion. Liz, I wanted to gather the whole haunted valley and lay it in your hands: the thunderheads like grieving horses, the heather’s purple smoke, the moon rising late with its face washed raw, but the dream would not stay still; it slipped, it shone, it broke into a thousand mirrored birds, and each bird carried away a fragment of sorrow so bright it could not be touched, only followed, farther and farther, into the beautiful and merciless distance where love, having no body, becomes the weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
